**6.3 Duality of Differential Kinematics and Statics**

We have found that the equivalent joint torques are related to the endpoint force by the

Jacobian matrix, which is the same matrix that relates the infinitesimal joint displacements to the

end-effecter displacement. Thus, the static force relationship is closely related to the differential

kinematics. In this section we discuss the physical meaning of this observation.
The lower half of Figure 6.3.1 is the linear mapping associated with the static force

relationship given by eq.(6.2.4). Unlike differential kinematics, the mapping of static forces is

given by the transpose of the Jacobian, generating a mapping from the *m*-dimensional vector

space ***V***^***m***, associated with the Cartesian coordinates of the end-effecter, to the *n*-dimensional

vector space *V*^*n,* associated with the joint coordinates. Therefore the joint torques τ are always
the orthogonal complement of *N*(**J**), then the range space *R*(**J**^T) is identical to *S1*, as shown in the

figure. Also, space *S3*, i.e., the orthogonal complement of *R*(**J**^T) is identical to *N*(**J**). What this

implies is that, in the direction in which joint velocities do not cause any end-effecter velocity, the

joint torques cannot be balanced with any endpoint force. In order to maintain a stationary

configuration, the joint torques in this space must be zero.

In general, satisfying equation (2.27) is not enough to ensure that a robot can be statically stable. The joint torques that are required to hold the posture must be within the physical capabilities of the robot, namely, its torque limits. We denote \(\tau_{i}^{-}\) and \(\tau_{i}^{+}\) the minimal and maximal torques that can be generated by the robot's actuators on joint \(J_{i}\). In some cases, the torque limits can depend on the joint parameters \(\tau_{i}^{-}(q)\) and \(\tau_{i}^{+}(q)\). For example, it is the case with the Atlas robot that is hydraulically actuated.

Featherstone [17] proposes a recursive algorithm to compute the torques, accelerations, and velocities generated in a multi-articulated system by a set of external forces called the Inverse Dynamics Algorithm. For the purpose of generating statically stable postures, the velocities and accelerations are not needed. Thus, we devise a specialized algorithm to fit our needs and call it the Inverse Static Algorithm.

# Chapter 3

# Control Algorithms for Grasping

## 3.1 The grasping control problem

The grasping control problem can be broken into two parts

1. Tracking – the center of mass of the object should follow a specified trajectory.

2. Holding – the finger forces should lie within the friction cone at all times.

Condition 2 is important not only because we do not wish to lose our grip on the object, but also because we assumed in our derivation of the grasp dynamics that contact was maintained. Without this constraint we would have to specify the dynamics of contact.

## Authors

Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. A single pendulum is swung up by energy control, which puts it on the homoclinic orbit that ends upright [1]. The double pendulum is chaotic [2], so energy control alone most likely ends in chaotic motion, and energy-based swing-ups of double pendulums pass through intermediate equilibria [3, 4]. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

keenable.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
keenable.snippet:
We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint.

Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3^∘ and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings.

We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

keenable.title: Hybrid control strategy for robust global swing-up of the pendubot
keenable.snippet:
The pendubot is a two-link underactuated mechatronic device frequently used for research in nonlinear control and robotics. As shown in Figure 1, the pendubot consists of a two-link planar robot arm (two coupled pendulums) with only one torque actuator at link 1. The pendubot is equipped with two optical sensors that measure angles at the joints. Each joint can fully rotate 360 degrees without any constraints on their motion. The pendubot has a total of four equilibrium configurations defined by the angular position and velocity of its links: both links resting (A r ), link 1 resting and link 2 upright (A ru ), link 1 upright and link 2 resting (A ur ), and both links upright (A u ).
One control challenge for the pendubot system is robust global stabilization of the upright configuration A u . While, several control strategies such as energy pumping [2], [4], jerk control [1], trajectory tracking [6], and hybrid control [9] have been proposed in previous years to solve the pendubot swing-up problem, the first provable robust and global feedback stabilizer stems from the hybrid control strategy in [7].

keenable.snippet: This paper studies nonlinear control of a 3-link planar robot moving in the vertical plane with only the first joint being actuated while the two other revolute joints are passive (called the APP robot below). A nonlinear energy-based controller is proposed, whose objective is to drive the APP robot into an invariant set where the first link is in the upright position and the total mechanical energy converges to its value at the upright equilibrium point (all three links are in the upright position). By presenting and using a new property of the motion of the APP robot, without any condition on its mechanical parameters, this paper proves that if the control gains are larger than specific lower bounds, then only a measure-zero set of initial conditions converges to three strictly unstable equilibrium points instead of converging to the invariant set. This paper presents numerical results for a physical 3-link planar robot to validate the obtained theoretical results and to demonstrate a switch–and–stabilize maneuver in which the energy-based controller is switched to a linear state feedback controller that stabilizes the APP robot at its upright equilibrium point.

However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design.

We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint.

Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. The direct-drive motors of the planar two-link robot of Fig. 1 deliver only 1.1 Nm, about 6 % of the gravity torque in the first joint with the arm held horizontally. With full torque in both joints, link 2 tilts by 16.3^∘ and link 1 stays hanging, because the reaction of the elbow torque cancels the shoulder torque (Fig. 1b). Neither a joint PD controller nor a controller that tracks a direct path to the upright pose (Fig. 5a) can get there; the robot has to collect the energy over many swings.

We instead guide the swing-up along the NNMs of the robot [5, 6, 7], families of periodic orbits of the free dynamics, one per energy. On one mode the robot behaves much like a single pendulum: there is no chaos, and the modes connect the hanging equilibrium to a homoclinic orbit at the upright one [8]. Pumping energy along a mode thus carries the robot from rest to almost upright, where a short precomputed trajectory catches it in a handstand.

keenable-realtime.title: Hybrid control strategy for robust global swing-up of the pendubot
keenable-realtime.snippet:
The pendubot is a two-link underactuated mechatronic device frequently used for research in nonlinear control and robotics. As shown in Figure 1, the pendubot consists of a two-link planar robot arm (two coupled pendulums) with only one torque actuator at link 1. The pendubot is equipped with two optical sensors that measure angles at the joints. Each joint can fully rotate 360 degrees without any constraints on their motion. The pendubot has a total of four equilibrium configurations defined by the angular position and velocity of its links: both links resting (A r ), link 1 resting and link 2 upright (A ru ), link 1 upright and link 2 resting (A ur ), and both links upright (A u ).
One control challenge for the pendubot system is robust global stabilization of the upright configuration A u . While, several control strategies such as energy pumping [2], [4], jerk control [1], trajectory tracking [6], and hybrid control [9] have been proposed in previous years to solve the pendubot swing-up problem, the first provable robust and global feedback stabilizer stems from the hybrid control strategy in [7].

keenable-realtime.title: Global motion analysis of energy-based control for 3-link planar robot with a single actuator at the first joint
keenable-realtime.snippet: This paper studies nonlinear control of a 3-link planar robot moving in the vertical plane with only the first joint being actuated while the two other revolute joints are passive (called the APP robot below). A nonlinear energy-based controller is proposed, whose objective is to drive the APP robot into an invariant set where the first link is in the upright position and the total mechanical energy converges to its value at the upright equilibrium point (all three links are in the upright position). By presenting and using a new property of the motion of the APP robot, without any condition on its mechanical parameters, this paper proves that if the control gains are larger than specific lower bounds, then only a measure-zero set of initial conditions converges to three strictly unstable equilibrium points instead of converging to the invariant set. This paper presents numerical results for a physical 3-link planar robot to validate the obtained theoretical results and to demonstrate a switch–and–stabilize maneuver in which the energy-based controller is switched to a linear state feedback controller that stabilizes the APP robot at its upright equilibrium point.

keenable-realtime.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
keenable-realtime.snippet: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design.

This paper focuses on the specific problem of balance maintenance during upright stance which is to be distinguished from balance maintenance during gait. We take our cue from biomechanics research [10] which points out the very different nature of the two apparently related problems and how human beings employ specific control strategies to deal with them.

They are minimized when the gravity forces are passively supported by the structure of the robot rather than being actively compensated by the joint motors. Such a posture would greatly reduce the energy expenditure, as we experience from our effortless upright stance compared to one with a bent knee.

# Push, Press, Slide: Mode-Aware Planar Contact Manipulation via Reduced-Order Models  
## Abstract  
Non-prehensile planar manipulation, including pushing and press-and-slide, is critical for diverse robotic tasks, but notoriously challenging due to hybrid contact mechanics, under-actuation, and asymmetric friction limits that traditionally necessitate computationally expensive iterative control. In this paper, we propose a mode-aware framework for planar manipulation with one or two robotic arms based on contact topology selection and reduced-order kinematic modeling. Our core insight is that complex wrench-twist limit surface mechanics can be abstracted into a discrete library of physically intuitive models. We systematically map various single-arm and bimanual contact topologies to simple non-holonomic formulations, e.g. unicycle for simplified press-and-slide motion. By anchoring trajectory generation to these reduced-order models, our framework computes the required object wrench and distributes feasible, friction-bounded contact forces via a direct algebraic allocator. We incorporate manipulator kinematics to ensure long-horizon feasibility and demonstrate our fast, optimization-free approach in simulation across diverse single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks. Supplementary videos and additional information are available at: this https URL
Researchers from Middle East Technical University and Bilkent University have proposed a different approach called MACRO: Mode-Aware Contact manipulation with Reduced-Order models. Instead of treating every push as a generic, complex physics problem, they categorize common manipulation tasks into a library of "modes." Each mode is then simplified into a "reduced-order model"—a basic kinematic template like a car or a unicycle. This allows for extremely fast, algebraic control that ensures the robot can move objects precisely and reliably in real-time.

Reducing the complexity of higher order problems can enable solving them in
analytical ways. In this paper, we propose an analytic whole body motion
generator for humanoid robots. Our approach targets inexpensive platforms that
possess position controlled joints and have limited feedback capabilities. By
analysing the mass distribution in a humanoid-like body, we find relations
between limb movement and their respective CoM positions. A full pose of a
humanoid robot is then described with five point-masses, with one attached to
the trunk and the remaining four assigned to each limb. The weighted sum of
these masses in combination with a contact point form an inverted pendulum. We
then generate statically stable poses by specifying a desired upright pendulum
orientation, and any desired trunk orientation. Limb and trunk placement
strategies are utilised to meet the reference CoM position. A set of these
poses is interpolated to achieve stable whole body motions. The approach is
evaluated by performing several motions with an igus Humanoid Open Platform
robot. We demonstrate the extendability of the approach by applying basic
feedback mechanisms for disturbance rejection and tracking error minimisation. cs.RO Grzegorz Ficht, Sven Behnke

In this work, the hierarchical control strategy of template-based control for
a bipedal robot is described. The axial force of a compliant leg is redirected
to a point, called the virtual pivot point (VPP), of a 2D biped robot, which is
located above the CoM of the model, to generate a restoring moment for the
trunk motion. The resulting behavior of the model would resemble a virtual
pendulum rotating around this VPP, thus aiming for an upright trunk during
walking. Inspired by this analysis, we propose a new force redirecting method
as a controller for robot walking. Then, these key features of the BTSLIP model
with a simple force direction controller are mapped into the overall input
torques of an articulated body robot via a task space controller. We consider a
full dynamic simulation of a 2D articulated body robot to validate the
performance of the proposed method under the random initial conditions and the
presence of force disturbances and moderately rough surfaces. Moreover, with
our control strategy, the robot achieves a stable walking motion while keeping
its upper body upright without using optimization methods. We hypothesize by
taking the advantage of the properties of mechanical templates, also called the
reduced-order model, this could enable stable gait for the full model robot
without the need for precise path planning. cs.RO Minh Nhat Vu

Static balancing of planar articulated robots
Giuseppe QUAGLIA , Zhe YIN
Front. Mech. Eng. ›› 2015, Vol. 10 ›› Issue (4) : 326 -343.
Static balancing of planar articulated robots
Static balancing for a manipulator’s weight is necessary in terms of energy saving and performance improvement. This paper proposes a method to design balancing devices for articulated robots in industry, based on robotic dynamics. Full design details for the balancing system using springs are presented from two aspects: One is the optimization for the position of the balancing system; the other is the design of the spring parameters. As examples, two feasible balancing devices are proposed, based on different robotic structures: The first solution consists of linkages and springs; the other consists of pulleys, cross mechanisms and (hydro-) pneumatic springs. Then the two solutions are compared. Pneumatic, hydro-pneumatic and mechanical springs are discussed and their parameters are decided according to the requirements of torque compensation. Numerical results show that with the proper design using the methodology presented in this paper, an articulated robot can be statically balanced perfectly in all configurations. This paper therefore provides a design method of the balancing system for other similar structures.

Worked Example 1 used the all-horizontal pose because it maximizes the torques, but a real arm spends most of its life in other configurations, and each joint's torque rises and falls as the pose changes. The general statement is that gravity torque about a horizontal axis depends on the horizontal offset of each carried mass, which for a link at angle θ θ from horizontal scales as cos θ cosθ . Tilt a link up toward vertical and its contribution to downstream joint torque falls toward zero; bring it back to horizontal and the contribution returns to full.

This is why a robot folding its arm in tight to its body, "tucking," dramatically reduces every joint torque — the masses move close to the axes and high, shortening the horizontal moment arms. It is also why the most dangerous pose for actuator sizing is rarely the one the robot uses most often.

...

The cosine factor also explains a phenomenon that surprises operators: a joint's torque can change sign as the arm sweeps through vertical. Consider the elbow holding a forearm that swings from pointing up-and-out, through horizontal, to down-and-out. On one side of horizontal the forearm's weight tends to fold the elbow closed; on the other side it tends to open it. At the exact horizontal the moment arm is maximum and the torque peaks; as the link approaches vertical above or below, the torque passes through zero and reverses direction. The actuator must be able to drive torque in both directions, and the gearbox sees the load reverse, which matters for backlash and for any drive component that behaves differently in two directions. seltz.title: Static Joint Torque for a Serial Robot Arm | Mech Codex
seltz.snippet:
Static joint torque is the holding torque each actuator in a serial robotic arm must develop to support the arm's own weight and any payload at a given configuration, and it sets the minimum motor sizing before any dynamic loads are added. Each joint must balance the gravitational moment produced by all links and masses outboard of it, so the calculation begins at the tool and works inward toward the base, summing link weights and their moment arms. This analysis governs motor and gearbox selection in industrial manipulators, collaborative robots, and custom automation where gravity loading at extreme reach can exceed inertial loads at operating speeds.

## Key Formula — Gravity Torque at Joint i by Outward Summation

τᵢ^grav = g ∑_k=iⁿ m_k \| r_i → c_k × hatzᵢ,perp \|

Where:

- τᵢ^grav — static (gravity-hold) torque the actuator at joint i must supply, in N·m
- g — gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s²
- m_{k} — mass of link k (or the payload, when k=n denotes the end mass), in kg
- r_i → c_k — vector from joint i's axis to the centre of mass of link k, in m
- hatzᵢ — unit vector along joint i's rotation axis; the cross product extracts the moment arm perpendicular to it
- n — total number of links/masses distal to (outboard of) the base; the sum runs only over everything that joint i actually carries

The whole article is one idea worked from every angle: a revolute joint feels the weight of everything beyond it, multiplied by how far out that weight sits, measured perpendicular to the joint's own axis. Sum those contributions from the wrist inward and you have the static torque map of the entire arm. Every later refinement — worst-case pose search, the Jacobian-transpose generalization, gearbox margin — is built on this sum.

Gravity torque at a robot joint is the moment that the weight of all links and the held payload creates about that joint axis, and it sets the minimum continuous torque the actuator must supply just to hold position. In serial manipulators, the gravity torque is pose-dependent and reaches its maximum when the arm is fully extended horizontally, which defines the worst-case sizing condition for joint motors and gearboxes. Ignoring end-effector payload mass is a common source of motor undersizing in collaborative robot applications where tooling weight is a significant fraction of rated arm payload.

## Key Formula — Static Gravity Torque About a Joint Axis

τ_J = g∑ᵢ mᵢ rᵢ

Where:

- τ_J — gravity (holding) torque the joint must resist, about its rotation axis (N·m)
- g — gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s² (use the local value if it matters; it rarely does)
- m_{i} — mass of the i-th contributor: payload, end-effector, wrist, forearm, upper arm (kg)
- r_{i} — horizontal distance from the joint axis to the center of mass of m_{i} in the current pose (m)
- The sum runs over every mass that hangs *outboard* of the joint you are sizing — everything the joint has to hold up against gravity

This is nothing more than the moment balance you learned in statics, written for a serial robot arm: each mass exerts a moment about the joint equal to its weight times its horizontal lever arm, and the joint actuator has to supply the equal and opposite moment to hold the pose. Every gravity-torque number in robot sizing — shoulder, elbow, wrist — is a specialization of this one line. The dynamic, inertial, and gearbox sections that follow either refine the lever arms, add a second torque term for acceleration, or transform the result back to the motor shaft. Get this moment balance right and the rest is bookkeeping.

The manipulator Jacobian is the matrix that links how fast a robot's joints move to how fast its tool moves in space. Every industrial robot, surgical arm, and legged machine relies on it: the moment a controller has to convert a desired Cartesian velocity into motor commands, or a commanded tip force into joint torques, the Jacobian is the object doing the translation. Robotics engineers meet it the first time they try to make an end-effector travel in a straight line and discover that constant joint speeds produce curved, accelerating tool paths instead. The Jacobian matters because it is simultaneously the velocity map, the diagnostic for singular configurations where the arm loses the ability to move in some direction, the source of the manipulability measure that quantifies how "nimble" a pose is, and — through a beautiful duality — the map from external forces to the joint torques needed to resist them. ## I. Orientation: Mechanical Description of Robot Motion

Robot mechanical design is governed by rigid-body motion, geometric constraints, and the relationship between forces, torques, and motion. Robot kinematics describes motion without considering forces; robot dynamics explains motion produced by forces and torques. A robot manipulator is modeled as a chain of rigid links connected by revolute or prismatic joints.

- **Rigid-body assumption:** Each link maintains constant shape and dimensions; deformation is neglected in basic analysis.
- **Reference convention:** A base frame is fixed to the robot, while link frames move with individual joints.

- **Pose representation:** A robot end-effector pose combines position and orientation, usually represented by a (4 \times 4) homogeneous transformation matrix.
- **Degrees of freedom:** The number of independent joint variables determines the robot's configuration freedom.
- **Units and signs:** Angles use radians in equations, distances use metres, forces use newtons, and torques use newton-metres.

## 03.01. Biped Locomotion Challenges Inverted Pendulum

Biped locomotion is fundamentally difficult because a humanoid must continuously control an unstable body while alternating between small and changing support regions. Unlike wheeled robots with persistent ground contact, a biped repeatedly transfers its weight from one foot to the other. Every step changes the contact geometry, available ground reaction forces, and mechanical constraints, requiring balance and motion generation to operate as one tightly coupled control problem.

The human-like body structure places a relatively large mass above narrow feet, producing dynamics similar to an inverted pendulum. In a conventional pendulum, gravity naturally restores the mass toward a stable hanging configuration. In an inverted pendulum, gravity instead amplifies deviations from the upright state. A humanoid must therefore generate continuous corrective motion through ankle torque, body acceleration, momentum regulation, and foot placement to prevent divergence.

The Center of Mass (CoM) provides a useful reduced representation of whole-body motion. Although a humanoid contains many articulated links, its global balance can often be interpreted through the relationship between the CoM, support contacts, and ground reaction forces. When the CoM moves relative to the support region, the controller must regulate contact forces and future footholds so that the resulting acceleration remains compatible with the intended locomotion behavior.

ultimate.snippet:
We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6 % of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint.

Swinging up a robot whose motors cannot even hold its arm horizontal is a matter of timing, not of force. ultimate.title: Hybrid control strategy for robust global swing-up of the pendubot
ultimate.snippet:
The pendubot is a two-link underactuated mechatronic device frequently used for research in nonlinear control and robotics. As shown in Figure 1, the pendubot consists of a two-link planar robot arm (two coupled pendulums) with only one torque actuator at link 1. The pendubot is equipped with two optical sensors that measure angles at the joints. Each joint can fully rotate 360 degrees without any constraints on their motion. The pendubot has a total of four equilibrium configurations defined by the angular position and velocity of its links: both links resting (A r ), link 1 resting and link 2 upright (A ru ), link 1 upright and link 2 resting (A ur ), and both links upright (A u ).
One control challenge for the pendubot system is robust global stabilization of the upright configuration A u . While, several control strategies such as energy pumping [2], [4], jerk control [1], trajectory tracking [6], and hybrid control [9] have been proposed in previous years to solve the pendubot swing-up problem, the first provable robust and global feedback stabilizer stems from the hybrid control strategy in [7].

ultimate.title: Global motion analysis of energy-based control for 3-link planar robot with a single actuator at the first joint
ultimate.snippet: This paper studies nonlinear control of a 3-link planar robot moving in the vertical plane with only the first joint being actuated while the two other revolute joints are passive (called the APP robot below). A nonlinear energy-based controller is proposed, whose objective is to drive the APP robot into an invariant set where the first link is in the upright position and the total mechanical energy converges to its value at the upright equilibrium point (all three links are in the upright position). By presenting and using a new property of the motion of the APP robot, without any condition on its mechanical parameters, this paper proves that if the control gains are larger than specific lower bounds, then only a measure-zero set of initial conditions converges to three strictly unstable equilibrium points instead of converging to the invariant set. This paper presents numerical results for a physical 3-link planar robot to validate the obtained theoretical results and to demonstrate a switch–and–stabilize maneuver in which the energy-based controller is switched to a linear state feedback controller that stabilizes the APP robot at its upright equilibrium point.

ultimate.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
ultimate.snippet: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design.
